Without using something like a camera, or at least a photomultiplier like in old nightvision goggles (where with the help of a battery or something, photons hitting a surface emit some electrons that hit a phosphor, that in turn lights up brighter than the incoming light; there is a bit more to it, but that's the gist of it); as far as I know it is not possible with the materials we currently have.

Assuming we could get materials with whatever properties we want; what you would have to do would be: First split the incoming light in 3 ranges (reflecting the sensitivity of the 3 types of color sensing cells we got in our eyes). Then for each range, use a beamsplitter to divide it into 3 separated beams. Then for each two out of three, for each range, send them to a surface with the required "phosphorescence" to "shift" the frequency up or down as required (as far as I know, we don't got phosphors that shift the frequency up, only down, so to get blue from green, and green and blue from red, we would need an yet undiscovered material). Now with the 9 beams (red, red-to-green, red-to-blue; green, green-to-red, green-to-blue; blue, blue-to-red, blue-to-green), you need to figure first which one of each set comes out dimer and add a filter to dim the others of the same set to balance, and then which of the sets is dimmer and filter down the others as well. And finally, use some beamsplitters to recombine everything (just arrange them backwards from what you would to split).

Alternatively, just dim the lights a lot; we don't see color very well in the dark (but then, we don't see anything very well in the dark)
